The Cook Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of competitiveness in U.S. congressional districts, based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy (now FairVote) in 1997. The index is updated every two years by The Cook Political Report. In 2021, the newsletter ended its relationship with Polidata and instead used Dave Leip's Atlas of U.S. Presidential Elections to calculate the 2020 results. The most recent iteration is the 2022 Cook PVI, which was released with an updated formula for calculating PVI values.

The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican) indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received. In 2022, the formula was updated to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

In healthcare settings, transgender individuals may face discrimination in the form of "trans broken arm syndrome," in which doctors mistakenly assume that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care and consequently treat their problem incorrectly or deny them care entirely. Trans patients often hide their trans status when visiting a doctor if their problem, such as a broken arm, isn't related to their trans status. A 2022 survey from the Center for American Progress revealed that 19 percent of trans individuals had experienced this form of discrimination in the past year.

Transgender people have the right to medical privacy. According to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing any personal medical information, including a person's transgender status. HIPAA also allows transgender people to access and receive a copy of their medical records from health care facilities. Insurance coverage for gender-affirming care can vary widely and is often not covered by standard health insurance plans. Some states have laws requiring insurance companies to cover gender-affirming care, but these laws are not uniform and may not apply to all transgender individuals.
